summary: For ages 11–12: explain the main changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, sublimation) using the particle model, and read heating/cooling curves to find melting and boiling points from their flat regions. The high-value idea is the plateau: for a pure substance, during a change of state the temperature stays constant even while heating continues, because incoming energy overcomes the forces holding particles in their arrangement rather than increasing particle speed (mixtures such as wax or chocolate tend to melt over a range of temperatures instead). Learners also distinguish evaporation (from the surface, at any temperature) from boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point), and see cooling as the mirror image with the same particles throughout (conservation). Keep energy qualitative — no latent-heat calculations.
misconceptions: Temperature keeps rising during melting/boiling even though heat is still added (missing the latent-heat plateau).
Evaporation and boiling are the same thing.
Boiling bubbles are air or oxygen rather than the substance's own vapour.
Freezing 'adds cold' rather than removing energy.
Particles are created or destroyed, or change size, during a state change (rather than only rearranging and changing speed).

activities.title: Change-of-state studio: link heating, particles, and the curve
steps: Use a heat/cool control and watch three linked panels together: a heat source, a beaker of particles, and a temperature-vs-time graph that draws itself as time passes.
Crank up the heat on a solid and observe the particles vibrate harder, then at the melting point break loose and move past one another as a liquid — and note that exactly there the graph goes flat.
Keep the heat full on during the flat region and read the thermometer: notice it refuses to climb during melting even though heating continues.
Continue heating to the boiling plateau, then run a cooling trace and watch the mirror-image curve form while tracking that the same particles persist throughout.
Toggle between a surface-evaporation mode (slow, at any temperature) and a boiling mode (bubbles of the substance's own vapour forming throughout the liquid at the boiling point) and compare.
Explore sublimation as a direct solid-to-gas change.
activities.insight: During a change of state the temperature holds constant because energy goes into rearranging particles (overcoming the forces holding them in their arrangement) rather than increasing their speed; the flat regions of the curve mark the melting and boiling points. Evaporation and boiling differ (surface/any temperature vs throughout/at the boiling point), and the same particles persist throughout.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: heating crushed ice
steps: Before doing anything, predict the temperature-vs-time graph for a thermometer in crushed ice that is heated steadily — especially what happens while ice and water coexist — and write WHY you predict that shape.
Heat crushed ice (taken to start at 0°C) steadily, stirring gently, with a thermometer in it and record the temperature over time, plotting the trace.

Compare your prediction with your real trace, which should show an approximately flat region at or near 0°C while ice and water coexist (a well-stirred mixture stays close to 0°C; small rises can happen if water near the heat source warms before all the ice has melted).
Explain where the heat energy 'goes' during the flat part, and answer: would freezing water show a flat part too, and at what temperature and why?
Apply the idea to a puzzle: wet clothes dry on a cold washing line — how, if water only turns to gas at 100°C?
activities.insight: The thermometer stays at about 0°C while ice and water coexist in a well-stirred mixture because the incoming energy overcomes the forces/arrangement holding the solid particles (changing state) rather than raising particle speed; only once all the ice has melted does the temperature rise clearly again. Evaporation from a surface occurs at any temperature, which is why cold wet clothes dry.

activities.title: Annotated heating/cooling curve reference
steps: Study a labelled heating and cooling curve with the flat regions marked as the melting and boiling points.
Reveal 'why temperature is constant' explanations attached to each flat region, and match each segment to a paired particle snapshot (solid vibrating, melting, liquid, boiling, gas).
Use this as a paper/reference consolidation after the studio activity: practise reading melting and boiling points off a curve and stating what particles are doing in each region.
activities.insight: A heating or cooling curve can be read for melting and boiling points at its flat regions, with each region corresponding to a specific particle behaviour and a reason for constant temperature during a change of state.

activities.title: Check: name, describe, read, and explain state changes
steps: Read a heating curve and identify the melting point and boiling point from the flat regions (e.g. using a slider or by labelling).
Match each state change (melt, freeze, boil, condense, sublime) to its correct particle-level description.
Sequence the states a substance passes through as it is heated or cooled.
Explain in your own words why temperature stays constant during a change of state, and distinguish evaporation from boiling.
activities.insight: Consolidates naming each change of state, describing the particle behaviour, reading melting/boiling points from a curve, and explaining the plateau mechanism and the evaporation/boiling distinction.

checkQuestion: I keep a thermometer in a beaker of crushed ice and heat it steadily. The ice starts at 0°C. While the ice is still melting — some ice, some water in the beaker — what does the thermometer read: rising, falling, or stuck? Then the key part: explain WHY the temperature does that while ice and water are both present.
checkAnswer: The thermometer stays STUCK at 0°C while ice and water coexist. The heat energy going in is used to break the bonds/arrangement holding the solid particles — changing state — rather than to raise the temperature (particle speed). Only once all the ice has melted does the temperature start rising again. Full marks need 'energy goes into the state change, not into heating'.
